Uses the right processor and only documented methods, with bookmarks, depth checks, `seek()`, and `get_updated_html()`. The main adherence flaw is using plain opener-only `next_tag()` to scan the list subtree. Because default `next_tag()` skips closers, it cannot reliably observe the list boundary before trailing incomplete or unsupported markup. It also does not check the `set_bookmark()` return value.

verdict.failure_analysis: Failures were limited to trial-3. In `incomplete-token-after-closed-list`, the candidate counted the list but continued scanning with plain `next_tag()` until the global scan hit the trailing incomplete `<img`; it then treated `paused_at_incomplete_token()` as proof that the first list could not be scanned. The misconception is that a clean scan of a region requires a clean scan of the rest of the fragment. The relevant docs are `next_tag()` saying `tag_closers` defaults to `skip`, `Recipe: scan a region before editing its opener` recommending `next_token()`, `Recipe: test subtree membership and direct children` requiring a depth-boundary check immediately after `next_token()`, and `get_current_depth()` explaining that the element's own closer is the depth-drop boundary. In `unsupported-after-closed-list`, the same over-scan reached unsupported markup outside the already closed list and interpreted `get_last_error()` as invalidating the list scan. The docs correctly say unsupported markup aborts the processor, but they do not state strongly enough that the error check must be made after the intentionally bounded region scan, not after walking unrelated trailing markup. The successful trials show the docs did well on processor choice, multiple tag alternatives, bookmarks, direct-child depth checks, and reading updates with `get_updated_html()`; no trial hallucinated HTML API methods.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs define breadcrumbs and show exact path matching, but do not include a small example for the common predicate 'does the current element have any ancestor from this set?' Subjects had to infer that get_breadcrumbs() includes the current token and should be sliced or otherwise excluded for ancestor-only checks.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a general ancestor-membership example that inspects get_breadcrumbs(), excludes the current element, and checks for one or more ancestor tag names. Also note that breadcrumb query arrays match paths, not arbitrary-depth ancestor searches.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs document single-loop state tracking and virtual closers, but they do not clearly distinguish when manual stack state is appropriate versus when breadcrumbs/current depth should be preferred for structural predicates.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add guidance such as: use breadcrumbs or get_current_depth() for containment/ancestor questions; use manual state in a single next_token() loop when accumulating cross-token facts or custom aggregates.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs explain that tag_name is not a list of alternatives, and show filtering multiple names, but the structural-query example is only for one concrete breadcrumb path. This leaves a small gap for tasks combining 'one of several tag names' with 'any ancestor matching one of several tag names'.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a general example that scans all openers with next_tag(), filters get_tag() against a set, then combines that with breadcrumbs/current-depth checks for structural conditions.

verdict.failure_analysis: All trials passed all hidden cases: simple, thead-tbody, omitted-closers, markup-in-cells, entities-in-cells, no-table, first-table-only, and empty-cells. The docs did well on the key concepts: create_fragment() for BODY fragments; HTML Processor instead of Tag Processor when structure matters; next_token() for text-aware traversal; get_current_depth() for subtree boundaries; virtual/implied closing tokens for malformed or omitted table markup; and get_modifiable_text() as decoded text only after checking for #text tokens. The main near-miss was not a failure: candidates did not explicitly inspect get_last_error() or paused_at_incomplete_token(), but the docs frame that as a caller policy for read-only extraction, and the task did not require rejecting partial input.

verdict.failure_analysis: All trials passed all 8 hidden cases. The rendered docs did unusually well for this task: the WP_HTML_Processor overview explicitly says to prefer the HTML Processor when structure, BODY-fragment parsing, implied closing tags, or normalized output matter; the 'Recipe: collect DOM-style text from a subtree' section warns that ordinary text is only #text tokens and excludes comments plus SCRIPT/STYLE/TEXTAREA/TITLE opener text; get_modifiable_text() documents decoded text for #text and TITLE/TEXTAREA; and serialize_token() includes the exact general pattern needed for token-by-token rewrites with wrapper markup. The main near-miss was fallback policy. Candidates consistently used normalize($html) ?? $html on create failure or get_last_error(). That is not hallucinated, but it can silently abandon emitted wrappers or return non-normalized raw input if normalization fails. The docs do warn that normalize($html) starts over from the original bytes and that fallbacks are different policies, so this was not a failure in these trials, but the contract remains easy to under-specify in tasks and examples.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs say a null processor means no processor was created, but examples leave the fallback entirely to caller policy. Models tend to write normalize($html) ?? $html, which can return non-normalized input in a function whose contract promises normalized output.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a short guidance note distinguishing fallback choices for string-returning normalizers: fail closed with an empty string/null, return best-effort accumulated serialization, or return raw input only when byte preservation is explicitly more important than normalization.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs correctly warn that normalize($html) after a rewrite discards emitted changes, but this is easy to miss when handling get_last_error() after the loop.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a compact 'after the loop' decision table for token rewrites: success returns accumulated output; unsupported markup should use an explicit caller-defined fallback; normalize($html) is a restart from the original input and never includes emitted wrappers/skips/replacements.

doc_gaps.problem: The decoded-text contract is present, but it is split across text extraction and method reference sections. This task depended on using decoded text for matching and serialize_token() for canonical re-encoding.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a concise pair of examples showing that get_modifiable_text() returns decoded plaintext for #text while serialize_token() emits normalized encoded HTML for the same token, without suggesting a task-specific wrapper solution.

verdict.failure_analysis: All three trials passed all 6 hidden cases, and execution.json reported no _doing_it_wrong or trigger_error records. The docs worked well for this task: the Tag Processor overview explicitly recommends WP_HTML_Tag_Processor for flat, byte-preserving tag/class edits; next_tag() documents tag-name queries and ASCII case-insensitive matching; the bookmarks section directly explains that re-setting the same bookmark name moves it and is the supported idiom for tracking the last occurrence in one pass; add_class() documents appending/preserving existing classes; and get_updated_html() is clearly identified as the way to retrieve queued class edits while preserving untouched bytes. Near-misses were minor: candidates did not release bookmarks or check set_bookmark() return values, but with one literal bookmark in a short-lived function that does not create a practical misuse.

verdict.failure_analysis: No hidden/frozen cases failed in any trial. The docs worked well for this task because the Tag Processor overview explicitly says to use WP_HTML_Tag_Processor for flat, byte-preserving attribute edits, while the Usage section shows the direct constructor and next_tag() scanning pattern. The get_attribute_names_with_prefix() section directly exposes the needed operation and its example demonstrates uppercase source attributes returning lowercase names. The remove_attribute() section establishes the documented mutation primitive, and get_updated_html() explains that queued attribute edits are returned while untouched bytes are preserved. Near-misses: remove_attribute() is very terse, and get_attribute_names_with_prefix() could more explicitly say that returned lowercase names are intended to be valid inputs to attribute mutation methods such as remove_attribute(), including when the source attribute used different casing.

doc_gaps.problem: The section says it returns lowercase names matching a prefix and gives an uppercase-attribute example, but it does not state the operational consequence clearly: callers can pass those normalized names directly to mutation APIs even if the original source casing differed.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a contract sentence such as: Returned names are normalized to lowercase and may be passed directly to get_attribute(), set_attribute(), or remove_attribute(); attribute lookup and mutation are ASCII case-insensitive for HTML attributes.

doc_gaps.problem: The method description is sparse compared with set_attribute(). It does not restate important behavior useful for safe bulk-removal loops, especially no-op behavior for absent attributes and behavior with duplicate or case-variant attributes.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Expand the docblock with a short note that remove_attribute() is safe to call while matched on a tag opener, is a no-op when the target attribute is absent, accepts normalized lowercase names, and removes the matched attribute consistently regardless of source casing.

doc_gaps.problem: The overview strongly explains processor choice, but there is no compact general recipe for bulk attribute cleanup by name pattern, even though the API provides a dedicated prefix helper.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a general example of scanning all tags, obtaining attribute names by prefix, mutating each returned name, and returning get_updated_html(). Keep it generic, e.g. removing or rewriting all attributes with a caller-supplied data-* prefix.

verdict.failure_analysis: No hidden cases failed: all three trials passed all 7 cases. The docs did well on the core concepts needed for this task: the HTML Processor overview says to use WP_HTML_Processor when structure or normalized output matters; create_fragment() documents body-fragment parsing and null creation checks; next_token() documents that unclosed elements still produce closing tokens; and serialize_token() explicitly explains token-by-token rewrites, skipping wrapper openers and closers while preserving descendants. The near-miss is fallback handling: two trials described normalize($html) after a rewrite as a safe fallback, even though the serialize_token() section warns that normalizing the original input discards skipped or replaced tokens. This did not affect the frozen tests because no unsupported-parser abort occurred after spans had been skipped.

doc_gaps.problem: The anti-pattern warning is present, but candidates still treated normalize($html) as a safe recovery path after emitting a partial rewrite.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Strengthen the fallback contract: after a token-rewrite loop has emitted changes, normalize($html) restarts from the original bytes and must only be used when intentionally abandoning all rewrite effects; otherwise return the accumulated rewrite, return a sentinel, or fail closed.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs say it returns the matched tag name, but do not state clearly enough that it applies to both opener and closer tokens, including virtual closers produced by the HTML Processor.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a sentence that get_tag() returns the uppercase element name for both opening and closing tag tokens, including parser-generated closing tokens, and null for non-tag tokens.

doc_gaps.problem: The distinction between an unclosed element and an incomplete trailing syntax token is spread across several sections.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a concise cross-reference note: unclosed elements are completed by parser-generated closers during token walks, while incomplete trailing syntax is not visited and may be omitted from serialization.
